content.text: The altitude can only be boosted by supply craft visiting the ISS.
Why does the altitude decrease in the times between height boosts?
Momentum of the ISS is being transferred to air molecules.
The moon's gravity changes the net force on the ISS as it orbits Earth.
The decrease in altitude makes it possible for a supply craft to reach the ISS.
The total mass of the ISS changes with the deliveries from each supply craft.
At an altitude of about $405\,\mathrm{km}$ there is still a thin atmosphere, so the ISS is still colliding with air molecules even though the force from them is tiny.

A

At an altitude of about 405 km there is still a thin atmosphere. As the ISS orbits it collides with air molecules, which are given momentum and the ISS loses momentum. Reading on ammeter: Increases. Explanation: Increase in back emf.
Reading on ammeter: Decreases. Explanation: Increase in back emf.
Reading on ammeter: Increases. Explanation: Decrease in back emf.
Back emf is induced only while the coil is cutting magnetic flux, so ask what happens to it the moment the rotation of the coil stops.
The battery voltage and the circuit resistance do not change, so the current is set by the net voltage across the motor: $I = \dfrac{V - \varepsilon_{\text{back}}}{R}$.

With less opposition the current from the unchanged battery increases, so the ammeter reading increases.

content.text: A planet $X$ has twice the mass and twice the radius of Earth.
What is the magnitude of the gravitational acceleration close to the surface of planet $X$?
Close to the surface of a planet $g = \dfrac{GM}{R^{2}}$, so treat the mass and the radius as independent factors to be changed one at a time.
Doubling the mass doubles $g$, but doubling the radius divides $g$ by four because of the inverse square relationship.

$g = GM/R^{2}$. Doubling the mass doubles $g$; doubling the radius multiplies $g$ by $\frac{1}{4}$. Hence $g_X = 2 \times \frac{1}{4}g = \frac{1}{2}g$.

content.text: A hypothetical journey to a distant star might be accomplished in an astronaut's life span by travelling at relativistic speeds.
What is the key concept which underpins such a hypothetical journey?
From the frame of reference of the spacecraft making the journey, the distance to the star is less.
Clocks on the spacecraft run slower and hence the rate at which fuel is used for the journey is decreased.
Relativistic effects on the spacecraft reduce its mass, making it possible to accelerate to the speeds needed for such a journey.
The relativistic increase in the mass of the fuel on board makes it possible to complete a longer journey with less fuel.
Identify which of the three relativistic effects changes lengths measured along the direction of motion, and which changes the rate at which clocks and onboard processes run.
The effect that matters must be one that shortens the journey as it is measured by the astronaut, not merely the rate of fuel burn or the mass of the spacecraft.
A

Special relativity predicts that lengths along the direction of motion are contracted, so an astronaut in the spacecraft measures a shorter distance to the star than an observer on Earth. Length contraction is the key concept; time dilation affects clocks but does not reduce fuel consumption, and relativistic mass effects make high-speed travel harder, not easier.

Direction of force acting on WX: Reverses every 180 degrees. Direction of torque produced on the coil by the force acting on WX: Reverses every 180 degrees.
The split-ring commutator reverses the current in the coil every half turn, and that is precisely what keeps the coil turning in the same direction.
Because the current and the position of the side WX change at the same moment, ask whether the turning effect about the axis also reverses, or whether the two reversals cancel.
C

In a DC motor the current reverses in the coil every half turn as it passes the split-ring commutator, so the direction of the force on side WX reverses every $180^\circ$. The torque produced by that force, however, is in the same sense at all times because the coil is simultaneously moving to the opposite side of the axis - that is what keeps the motor turning in one direction. Hence option C.

content.text: A magnetic field is to be applied to make the electrons continue to travel in a straight line.
What is the magnitude and direction of the magnetic field that is to be applied?
$5 \times 10^{-1}\,\mathrm{T}$ into the page.
$5 \times 10^{-1}\,\mathrm{T}$ out of the page.
$1 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{T}$ into the page.
$1 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{T}$ out of the page.

Find the field between the plates from $E = \dfrac{V}{d}$ and hence the force on each electron from $F = qE$. The field is uniform, so without a magnetic field the electrons would accelerate along the field direction and their path would curve.
For a straight path the magnetic force must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so set $qvB = qE$ and use the left-hand rule, remembering to reverse it for a negative charge.
A

$E = V/d = 1000/0.001 = 1.0 \times 10^{6}\,\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$. The electric force on each electron is $F = qE = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 1.0 \times 10^{6} = 1.6 \times 10^{-13}\,\mathrm{N}$ and is vertically upwards (towards the positive plate). For a straight path the magnetic force must be vertically downwards, so $F = qvB$ gives $B = 1.6 \times 10^{-13}/(1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 2 \times 10^{6}) = 0.5\,\mathrm{T}$. For an electron moving to the right to be pushed downwards, the right-hand rule requires the field into the page.

content.text: In a thought experiment, the train is travelling from left to right fast enough relative to the tunnel that its length contracts and it fits inside the tunnel.
An observer on the ground sets up two cameras, at X and Y, to take photos at exactly the same time. The photos show that both ends of the train are inside the tunnel.

content.alt_text: Two photographs side by side, labelled Photo 1 (camera X) and Photo 2 (camera Y), each showing the front end of the train inside the tunnel mouth.

content.text: A passenger travelling on the train at its centre can see both ends of the tunnel and is later shown the photos.
From the point of view of the passenger, what is observed and what can be deduced about the photos?
The tunnel's length contracts so the train does not fit, and photo 2 is taken before photo 1.
The tunnel's length contracts so the train does not fit, and photos 1 and 2 are taken at the same time.
The tunnel appears to expand due to length contraction of the train, allowing it to fit in the tunnel, and photo 1 is taken before photo 2.
The tunnel appears to expand due to length contraction of the train, allowing it to fit in the tunnel, and photos 1 and 2 are taken at the same time.

Ask the question in each frame in turn. In the ground frame the train is length-contracted and fits. In the train's own frame it is the tunnel that is moving, so ask what happens to the tunnel's length and whether the train still fits.

Simultaneity is frame-dependent. The two cameras are at different positions in the ground frame, so use the Lorentz transformation $t' = \gamma\left(t - \dfrac{vx}{c^{2}}\right)$ to compare the times at which the two photographs were taken in the train's frame.
A
In the ground frame the moving train is length-contracted, so it does fit inside the tunnel, and both cameras sit in that one frame, so the two exposures really are at the same instant.

In the train's own frame it is the tunnel that is moving, so the tunnel is length-contracted. The train keeps its rest length, which is longer than the tunnel, so the train no longer fits and the passenger sees the ends of the train still outside the tunnel mouths. Nothing expands.

The order of the two exposures follows from the Lorentz time transformation $t' = \gamma\left(t - \dfrac{vx}{c^{2}}\right)$. Taking the origin at the centre of the tunnel, the exposures are simultaneous in the ground frame at $t = 0$, with camera X at the rear ($x_X = -d$) and camera Y at the front ($x_Y = +d$). Then $t'_X = +\dfrac{\gamma v d}{c^{2}}$ and $t'_Y = -\dfrac{\gamma v d}{c^{2}}$, so the exposure at Y happens first: photo 2 is taken before photo 1.
Only option A states both of these results, so A is the key.

Then find the force between that induced current and the field of the lower solenoid and apply it to the solenoid hanging from the spring balance. The force exists only while the current is changing, which is why the reading returns to its initial value.

The conventional current flows out of the positive terminal of the cell and through the lower solenoid. The current in the straight conductor must therefore flow from X to Y. Because the bus decelerates forwards, the mass continues to move forwards and ends up ahead of its original position, i.e. towards the front of the bus. content.text: When this action is carried out, the pointers on both meters move relative to the scales on the meters.
Which row of the table correctly identifies the movement of the pointer on Y and the reason for its behaviour?
Movement of pointer: Towards right. Reason: The movement of X produces a current that flows into the opposite terminal of Y.
Movement of pointer: Towards right. Reason: According to Lenz's law the effect produced must oppose the cause of the flux.
Movement of pointer: Towards left. Reason: Y behaves as a motor with the current flowing through it from right to left.
Movement of pointer: Towards left. Reason: For every force, there is an equal and opposite force.
Rotating meter X changes the magnetic flux linking its own coil, so for the moment of that rotation X behaves as a source and drives a current around the loop through Y.

Y is then carrying current, so it behaves as a motor: the direction of that current through Y's coil is what fixes the direction its pointer moves. Trace the current out of one terminal of X, along the connecting lead, and into a terminal of Y.
C

Turning meter X rotates its coil inside its own permanent magnet, so the flux linking X's coil changes during the rotation and an emf is induced in it. For the moment of the rotation X therefore acts as a source, driving a current around the circuit through meter Y - the same current that deflects X's own pointer.

That current passes through Y's coil in the field of Y's own magnet, so Y now behaves as a motor: the forces on the two sides of the coil produce a torque and the pointer swings away from zero. By Lenz's law the induced current flows in the sense that opposes the rotation, and the sense in which that current then passes through Y - set by the polarity of the interconnection in the paper's diagram - is what fixes the direction of Y's deflection. With the connection as printed the pointer of Y moves towards the left.

C is the only row that is right in both columns. A and B both state the direction as towards the right, and B additionally mis-states Lenz's law, which says the induced effect opposes the change in flux rather than 'the cause of the flux'. D states the correct direction but an invalid reason: the turning torque on Y's coil comes from Y's own field acting on the current in Y's coil, and is not the reaction partner of any force.

content.text: What is the magnitude and direction of the current in X?

The force between two parallel wires varies as $\dfrac{kI_1I_2}{d}$. Since the net force on Y is zero, the attraction to Z must be cancelled by a force from X, so set the two equal with the current in X as the unknown.

Fix the direction before the arithmetic: Y and Z attract, so they carry current the same way, and a repulsive force from X means the current in X must run the other way. Then get the magnitude from the balance.
$50\,\mathrm{A}$, travelling in the direction opposite to Y (that is, antiparallel to the currents in Y and Z).

Caution on the official key: the NESA 2018 HSC Physics marking guidelines sample answer for Q24(b) reads "50 A travelling in the same direction as Y". The magnitude is right, but a current in X running the same way as Y would attract Y, and that attraction would add to the attraction Z already produces, so the net force on Y could not be zero. Only an antiparallel current in X repels Y and can cancel the attraction. The physically consistent answer is given above; the divergence from the official wording is flagged for a human decision.

The force per unit length between two long parallel wires carrying currents $I_1$ and $I_2$ a distance $d$ apart is $F/L = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$, so it varies as the product of the currents and as the inverse of the separation (first power of $d$, not the inverse square law).

Only two wires act on Y, and its net force is zero, so the force from X must be equal in magnitude and opposite in type to the attraction from Z. With $I_Y = I_Z = 20\,\mathrm{A}$, $d_{XY} = 0.75\,\mathrm{m}$ and $d_{YZ} = 0.30\,\mathrm{m}$, cancelling the common current and the common constant gives

For the direction: parallel currents attract and antiparallel currents repel. Y and Z attract, so they carry their currents the same way. The attraction towards Z must be cancelled, so X must push Y away, which requires the current in X to run opposite to the current in Y. (A current in X running with Y would attract Y as well, and the two attractions would add rather than cancel.)

content.text: Outline the similarities and differences between the effects of electric fields and gravitational fields on matter. In your answer, refer to the definitions of these fields.

The $500\,\mathrm{km}$ is an altitude above the surface, but the denominator in $U = -GMm/r$ is the distance from the Moon's centre, so it becomes $1740 + 500 = 2240\,\mathrm{km}$.

Write the potential energy at each of the two radii before you subtract, and keep the negative sign on both of them. The change is the final value minus the initial value, and it comes out positive because the mass is moving further from the Moon.
$\Delta E_p = 1.26 \times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{J}$
Initial potential energy of mass: $E_{pi} = -\frac{GMm}{r_i} = -\frac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 7.35 \times 10^{22} \times 20}{1.74 \times 10^{6}} = -5.64 \times 10^{7}\,\mathrm{J}$.

content.text: Calculate the velocity of the $20\,\mathrm{kg}$ mass at an altitude of $500\,\mathrm{km}$.

content.text: How does light contribute to the flow of current in each of these two cells?

Work out, for each cell, whether an external battery is doing the collecting. In the vacuum photocell it is, so light has to do no more than start electrons moving and something else has to move them to the other electrode.

In the solar cell there is no battery, so the cell has to make its own potential difference. Ask where that comes from, and what the junction does to the electrons and the holes that the light creates in each of the two layers.

In the vacuum photocell photons eject electrons from photocathode A which are attracted to anode B by the battery; in the solar cell the p-n junction separates the photo-generated electrons and pushes them through the external circuit to the load.

In a vacuum photocell, incoming photons strike a photocathode A, knocking electrons out of its surface, which are attracted to an anode B due to the potential difference applied by the battery, thus producing a current.

In a solar cell, a potential difference is set up by the p and n junction. When incoming photons of light hit the electrons, the n-type semiconductor electrons are pushed through the external circuit, thus creating a current, which is electricity for the load.

content.text: Work through the system one section at a time from left to right: generator, T1, transmission lines, T2, houses, and ask what changes in each section when the houses draw more power.
Track three quantities separately: the voltages at each point, the current in each conductor, and the rate of energy loss as heat. You will need $P = VI$, $P_{loss} = I^2R$ and $V_p/V_s = N_p/N_s$.
The conductors have resistance, so a larger current produces a larger voltage drop along them. Follow that through to the voltage at the input and output of each transformer.

Current in the transmission lines and the power station output increases (approximately doubling if the house current doubles), heating losses in the wires and transformer cores increase, and the small voltage drops along the conductors increase so the transformer voltages fall slightly.
The increased demand for energy can be analysed in terms of the effect on voltages, current and energy losses.
Voltages: the output voltage from the power station, the transmission line voltage and the supply voltage to the houses remain approximately constant.

Current: an increase in the total current drawn from T2 by the houses produces an increase in the transmission line current and the output current from the power station. If the former doubles, then the transmission line current and the current output of the power station approximately double.

Energy losses: heat is produced in the transmission line wires and other wires due to their resistance. As the current increases the heat produced in the wires increases. Heat is also produced by eddy currents in the transformer cores, and this increases as the current increases.

Because of the resistance of the wires, relatively small voltage drops occur along these conductors and these increase as more appliances are turned on in the houses. This results in slight decreases in the voltage inputs and outputs at each of the transformers.
Answers could include: reference to parallel circuits in the houses.

content.text: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
Sub-part (a)(i) asks for specific uses, not general ones — name an organ and what is being detected in it.

Sub-part (a)(ii) is about what a very strong static field does to hydrogen nuclei before any radio frequency is applied. Consider their orientation, how many of the two possible alignments there are, and the direction of the resulting precession.

items: (a)(i) MRI is used to detect cancerous tissues and to distinguish between grey and white matter in the brain.

(a)(ii) Hydrogen nuclei in water molecules tend to align their spins with the field. The axes of rotation are not exactly parallel to the external field direction, and the spins of these protons precess around the direction of the applied external field at a rate that is dependent on the strength of the field. The hydrogen nuclei align parallel or antiparallel to the field, with a small minority in the parallel direction.

content.text: (a)(i) Two specific uses: detecting cancerous tissue, and distinguishing grey matter from white matter in the brain. Both exploit the fact that different tissues have different hydrogen content and different relaxation times.

(a)(ii) The applied field $B$ is static. The net spin of each hydrogen nucleus makes it behave as a tiny magnet, so in the field the nuclei adopt one of two alignments — with the field (lower energy, spin up) or against it (higher energy, spin down) — with a slight excess in the lower state.

Because the spin axis is not exactly along the field, each nucleus precesses about the field direction rather than pointing steadily at it. The precession rate (the Larmor frequency) is proportional to the field strength, so a stronger magnet produces a faster precession. It is this precession that the later radio frequency pulse is tuned to.

When ultrasound waves are reflected from a moving surface, the frequency of the reflected wave is higher if the surface is moving towards the incident wave and lower if it is moving away. Information about the angle between the directions of the velocities of the ultrasound and the reflecting surface can be determined to produce more accurate images.

content.text: Compare both the production and benefits of this CAT image with a conventional X-ray image of the same part of the person's body.
Structure the answer as two labelled halves — production and benefits — and make at least one explicit comparison in each half rather than describing the two techniques in isolation.

The key idea behind the production comparison is that a plain X-ray integrates everything in front of each point on the detector, while a CAT scan measures attenuation from many directions and reconstructs slices. The key idea behind the benefits comparison is what that does to clarity, ambiguity and soft-tissue differentiation.

A CAT scan uses a narrow rotating X-ray beam with a co-rotating detector and computer reconstruction to give a clear, unambiguous image with better soft tissue differentiation; a conventional X-ray uses a wide static beam giving a single longitudinal projection that can be ambiguous and is cheaper.
The production of both types of scans is dependent on differences in the absorption of X-rays passed through the body by different types and depths of tissue. Conventional X-rays are cheaper.

A conventional X-ray image of the neck is made by passing X-rays in a wide beam transversely through the neck, producing a longitudinal image of the neck in a single plane, which is the result of the absorption of the X-rays by all the intervening tissues. The image can be ambiguous.

In contrast to this, a CAT scan is produced by a narrow beam of X-rays that are passed through the person from a source that rotates in the transverse plane around the person's body, and which are detected by a sensor that also moves so that it is always opposite the X-ray source. This data is processed by a computer to produce an image that is a cross-section of the body. The benefit is that the CAT image is clearer and less ambiguous than the conventional X-ray image. The CAT scan also produces better soft tissue differentiation.

In the case of the CAT scan shown, it shows structures in the longitudinal plane, as would be the case with a conventional X-ray. This is achieved by combining multiple transverse images allowing computer software to produce an image in a single plane through the body at any angle.

content.text: The parsec and trigonometric parallax
Define the parsec with the aid of a diagram.

Trigonometric parallax measures how far a star appears to shift against distant background stars as Earth moves. The largest baseline available is the diameter of Earth's orbit, $1\,\mathrm{AU}$, obtained by observing six months apart.

The definition ties an angle to a distance: draw the $1\,\mathrm{AU}$ baseline, the sight line from the star, and the small angle the baseline subtends. Work out from your diagram what happens to that angle as the star gets further away.
For the limitations, work outwards from the telescope: name everything the atmosphere does to the light on its way in, then use your diagram to state which stars can be measured at all.
One parsec is the distance from Earth to a star whose annual parallax — the angle subtended by a $1\,\mathrm{AU}$ baseline — is one arcsecond.

The apparent position of a star is measured against distant background stars at two opposite points of Earth's orbit. The two observing positions are $1\,\mathrm{AU}$ apart, and the small angle at the star between the two sight lines is the annual parallax.

This is exactly the definition of the parsec: the distance at which a $1\,\mathrm{AU}$ baseline subtends an angle of one arcsecond. Because the angle is tiny, the relation between the angle and the distance is $d = \frac{1}{p}$ parsecs when $p$ is in arcseconds.

content.text: The parsec and trigonometric parallax
Outline TWO limitations of using ground-based instruments to make trigonometric parallax measurements.

The Earth's atmosphere refracts, scatters and distorts the incoming light, which limits the resolution of ground-based telescopes so small angles cannot be measured accurately; and because the parallax angle becomes smaller the further away the star is, only the nearest stars can be measured by this method.

Limitation 1: the atmosphere refracts light from its changing density and produces turbulence, so the image of a faint star is distorted and its position cannot be pinned down to the arcsecond precision that a small parallax angle demands. Limit the resolution of ground-based telescopes.

Limitation 2: from $d = \frac{1}{p}$, the parallax angle decreases as the distance increases, so beyond a few hundred parsecs the angle is far too small to be measured. Only the nearest stars can have their distances found this way, and other techniques must be used for the rest.

content.text: The Bohr model of the atom
Identify TWO limitations of the Bohr model of the atom.

For the limitations, test the model against what is actually observed: does it hold for hydrogen alone or for every element, and does it predict how bright each spectral line is as well as where the lines fall?

For the emission spectrum, begin from the model's central postulate — the electron may occupy only certain specific energy levels — and reason forward from what must happen for an electron to change level.

Remember that the quantity released in a transition is fixed by the difference between two levels, so only particular energies can be emitted. A labelled level diagram makes this obvious and earns credit.

The model works accurately only for hydrogen (and hydrogen-like ions) and not for atoms with more than one electron; and it accounts for the position of the spectral lines but not for their variation in intensity (nor for hyperfine structure or the Zeeman effect).

First limitation: the quantised energy levels are derived for a single electron orbiting a nucleus, so the model is quantitatively successful for hydrogen only and fails for helium and the heavier atoms.

Second limitation: the model predicts the energies of the emitted photons, hence the wavelengths of the lines, but not the intensities of those lines. It also ignores small splittings such as hyperfine structure and the Zeeman effect.

content.text: The Bohr model of the atom
How does the Bohr model of the atom account for the emission spectrum of hydrogen?

Electrons can occupy only specific quantised energy levels. When an excited electron falls to a lower level it emits a photon whose energy $hf$ equals the difference between the two levels, so only particular wavelengths are produced and a line spectrum rather than a continuous spectrum results.
In the Bohr model the electron occupies only particular energy levels. If an excited electron drops from level $E_2$ to a lower level $E_1$, the energy released leaves the atom as a single photon.

Because only certain energy differences are possible, only certain photon energies, and hence only certain wavelengths, can be emitted. That is why hydrogen gives a set of sharp emission lines at fixed wavelengths instead of a continuous spectrum.

content.text: Electric and electronic circuits; optical fibres
Outline TWO differences between an electric circuit and an electronic circuit.

For the comparison, first decide what each kind of circuit is optimising for — the power it delivers or the information it carries — and then build each difference from that: the voltage and current levels, and the resistance of the components used.

For silica, list what an optical fibre needs to achieve and match each need to a property of the material: it must form into a thin flexible strand, it must transmit light with very little loss, and the light must be kept inside the core.

For the last of those, remember that total internal reflection requires the core to have a higher refractive index than the surrounding cladding, so the question to ask is whether the refractive index can be controlled.

An electric circuit is designed to transmit power, so it uses high voltages and large currents; an electronic circuit carries information as signals and operates at low voltages and currents. Electric circuits contain devices such as lamps and motors whose resistance is small, whereas electronic circuits contain transistors and integrated circuits whose resistance is large, so currents and power losses are small.

Difference 1: purpose and therefore levels. An electric circuit is designed to deliver power, so it works at high voltage and current, while an electronic circuit represents information and works at low voltage and current.

Difference 2: components. The devices in power circuits — lamps, motors, heaters — have low resistance, so large currents flow. The devices in electronic circuits — transistors, integrated circuits, sensors — have high resistance, so currents and power losses are small.

content.text: Electric and electronic circuits; optical fibres
How do the properties of silica make it an ideal material for use in electronic communication?

Silica can be drawn into thin, flexible fibres at high temperature; it is optically transparent and can be made very pure, so attenuation over long distances is small; and its refractive index can be varied so the core has a higher index than the cladding, allowing total internal reflection to keep the light in the core.

Property 1: silica can be melted and drawn into very thin, flexible fibres, which is what makes an optical fibre possible at all. Property 2: it is transparent to visible and near-infrared light and can be purified to a very high level, so very little of the signal is absorbed and attenuation over long distances is small.

Property 3: the refractive index of silica is about 1.5 but can be varied by changing its composition, so the core can be given a higher index than the cladding. Light striking the core-cladding boundary beyond the critical angle is then totally internally reflected and stays in the core, even around bends.

An inverting amplifier is defined by where the two resistors go: one in series from the input to the $(-)$ terminal, the other from the output back to that same $(-)$ terminal. The $(+)$ terminal goes to ground, and no connection is made to the $(+)$ terminal from the input.

Begin with the problem: state why the electronic circuit cannot itself carry the high voltage or current without being destroyed.

Then separate the relay into its two sides — the low-power input side containing the electromagnet, and the high-power side containing the switch contacts — and state how energy gets from one to the other without an electrical connection between them.
Name the components and their roles individually: coil and soft iron core, armature or lever, pivot, and the contacts. A well-labelled diagram will earn credit here.

A small electronic current energises the relay's electromagnet, which pulls a pivoted lever that closes the mechanically isolated switch contacts, allowing a high-voltage, high-current circuit to be switched.

An electronic circuit cannot handle high voltages or currents without damaging components. Relatively small power is required to operate an electromagnet which forms the input of the relay. This electromagnet pulls a lever which, via a pivot, pushes a switch contact closed. The switch contacts are electrically insulated from the lever in order to isolate the output from the input. Since it is a mechanical switch, it can be manufactured to handle much higher voltages and currents. Answers may include: a well-labelled diagram.

content.text: Explain the operation of this circuit. Support your answer with a truth table and data from the thermistor characteristic curve.

Solve the sensor first. Work out the reference voltage set by the two fixed resistors, then find the thermistor resistance at which the input equals it. Because this is an NTC thermistor, resistance falls as temperature rises, which fixes a temperature threshold.
Read that threshold off the thermistor characteristic curve rather than assuming a value, and keep the figure consistent with the divider arithmetic.

Then identify each gate in turn and work out the logic from the isolation switch, the temperature signal and the smoke signal. Finish with a truth table covering every combination and state the single condition under which the alarm sounds.
The alarm sounds only when the isolation switch is open and either the temperature exceeds about 60 degrees Celsius or smoke is detected.

For the temperature sensor to produce a high output the input voltage must be greater than the reference voltage provided by the two fixed resistors. As the temperature rises $R_t$ will decrease, increasing the input voltage.
$R_t = \frac{10}{5.6}R = 2.8\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ so the input voltage equals the reference voltage. On the graph this corresponds to $60^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
Truth table (isolation switch, temperature high, smoke high -> alarm on): the alarm is activated only if the switch is open and either or both of the outputs ($T_{out}$, $S_{out}$) are high.
The alarm will be activated under the following conditions: the switch must be open and either the temperature is above $60^\circ$ or the smoke detector output is high.
